title: Rene Pajta - The Enterprise Version of the One Person Unicorn

segments.text: RENE PAJTA: Good morning, everybody.
This session will be slightly different
because we talked a lot about what we're building,
how we're improving all those technologies.
And I'm focused more about how these technologies
are adopted in the organizations, how
they are actually used.
With Vibe Engineering, we see a lot of things
being created, but struggling to get the adequate usage
and live through in the organizations.
I'm basically a Chief Architect at Microsoft
advising the CTOs and CIOs of Fortune 500 organizations.
I focus on their AI transformations and both
how to build with AI, but also how
to build agents which are worth to purchase and create
the new business models for them.
And also at the same time, running
as a technical lead our own sales
or customer success account transformation,
where we have around 700 people.
And we building our own agentic systems
to help us to run accounts better
and uplift the quality of how we run our own business.
And I would like to start maybe with a concept called enterprise
unicorn.
We heard about one person unicorns to be.
And this is a bit looking at what it takes,
maybe how that could look like in a larger organization which
has over 10,000 people, and what it will be as a shape and form
in there.
And I believe a lot of that going towards, rather than
talking about the headcount, is going
about how are we going to operate in, let's say,
a few years.
And I call it either mission control or a command center,
basically having a human, an agent,
a shared state where we have a pre-built signals based on which
we can act in the organizations even
before we ask the questions.
The chats are more things of dealing with exceptions
and trying to capture those as new signals, which
we have to make the decisions in the organizations.
And really, I would say, a simple test of this
will be that how many meetings we
will need to have to think internally as an organization?
In ideal state, we won't need those meetings
because everybody is on the same page
as we capture that intelligence within the organization.
And as usual, it all starts with the waves.
We started with chats, with assistants.
Now, we have the micromanagement management
of agents where we run the tasks.
They run for a while.
But then they still need our steering,
or we don't have developed the trust into them.
And we want to move to the delegation and remote execution.
What we see with promise of the open claw,
automated agents running parts of our businesses.
And I still would say that majority
or a lot of the enterprises, large organizations
are in that micromanage state because of a couple of things
that we just have access to the systems which
needs to be connected to really done the work.
For example, I'm a salesperson.
I need to connect to three to four different systems.
I need to have access to those combined that information,
to bring and build that one mission control system.
But that's not enough.
I need an intelligence how we as an organization are using that.
And that usually the vendors cannot build.
That needs to build by the organization internally.
And therefore, they are still, I would
say, in the micromanagement state
because we have those connectors,
but that company intelligence still
needs to be developed in the organization.
So I would say, moving to the delegation piece
will really require that wider system
access to have all that information to bring it
in one place.
Plus, the tacit knowledge of the organization
to develop the trust on top of those workflows.
And because of how, let's say, the technology evolves.
We see new models every three months.
We see new frameworks, harnesses to being positioned.
The CIs and CTOs have really tough questions there.
Like, how I find the clear direction,
how I bet on what technologies to evolve and upskill
my organization to survive such waves of different technologies.
Imagine, if you have 10 people in your organization,
it's pretty much a daily business
to also learn and adjust.
However, if you have an organization of 10,000 people,
it requires a lot of coordination efforts,
communication, enablement strategy.
And if there is no clear direction to that, usually, what
happens is either people wait, or they
start building on their own, which
then creates one part is just stalled organization.
The other one is basically creating a shadow IT
with engineering that's even booming.
And then it's very difficult to create a governance.
Ideally, the companies wants to operate
like a small city with clear laws,
but also freedom to experiment within those boundaries.
And that's also where the efforts then going really
in terms of standardization.
We need to have standardization in terms of the governance,
in terms of the policies.
We do have to enable those laws to be around, and then
allow those on the edge actually to build and innovate.
Because there is that tacit knowledge
captured in the organization.
We don't centrally.
Let's say, in the organization what's happening,
what are the nuances, how the organization operates.
And we need to have both of those.
So a lot of questions come to what I buy
and what I build, where is the mode,
and where is a commodity in that space.
And I would say, what we are a lot see,
the models, the agent harness, the connectors,
that's all a commodity which you ideally focus on buying.
But then, really, the mode for the organization
is their company intelligence, how
I capture that intelligence of my organization.
And an example from our side is, we have a reporting system,
which has around 400 reports.
I have a connector to it.
But that connector is just giving me access
to go and query those reports.
However, what I need to do is really
to understand how my expert teams are using those reports.
When they use what.
And that's basically what we also
do as a one layer is just the connector itself.
The other one is going and crawling those systems,
creating kind of navigation like mental model,
capturing how my employees are going and retrieving
that information.
Because that allows me to actually
have agents which I can trust, have agents
which are making less mistakes.
They are not this junior intern employees.
They are experts.
And they're even better than I am in doing that job.
And that also then, with the latency and the cost,
actually reducing because they make less mistakes on achieving
that specific task.
And that's basically like where we're saying also
this company intelligence is something durable.
It's where you want to capture those nuances.
You can have let's say a global sales book that
can be shared globally.
But then, the nuances, how we handle, let's say,
our accounts in Germany or how the others handle accounts,
let's say, in Japan.
It's very different nuances, which
you can't globalize and generalize
and needs to be captured on that edge level.
And once you know what you want to build
and what you need to, let's say, buy,
it also comes with the operating model.
Meaning that you have that central spine where
you're building, let's say, the key connectors to the system.
You don't want to have your fields to go and do
the authentication and authorizations, integrations
to the key critical systems.
You want to have that done centrally so you provided access
to the data for the teams.
But then also on the other side, you
on the edge for your employees allowed to, let's say,
build around it.
They focus more on how to capture
the knowledge of that day-to-day task and operations.
Because if you have just everything centrally,
we create a global governance systems, but which are missing
work because they are not doing exactly what we on the edge
expect.
And on the other side, we just let everybody do the innovations
on the field side, we're creating and booming
the shadow IT, which is very difficult to govern.
And with that, I would say, coming back again to, let's say,
that one person unicorn, it won't be--
let's say, one person doing the work,
it will be everybody being a CEO in a boardroom,
having their own set of agents and workbenches, which
allow them to take the decisions on daily basis.
Imagine, I think our work will shift to the point
that we have a queue of, let's say,
your colleagues behind you asking you
questions on different topics, and you to make the decisions.
So it will come also with a new type of mental load on us.
We are not used to do decision making on a constant basis.
We are very difficult with content switching.
So these things will be creating challenges for us mentally,
as well how to adjust the work.
And also the trust will be very important.
Because if we can't trust our delegates who
do the work for us, we won't be able to make those decisions.
And those two things will be shifting,
and at least, what I see across the enterprises.
So if I should leave with one, it would be buy the models,
buy the commodity and build that intelligence layer
in your organizations.
Thank you.
[APPLAUSE]
